scripts.opening:opening:
[softly] JAUNT: THE WALK TO THE LAKE. Daybreak on a Monday in November 1904, at the south end of Prairie Avenue.

[short pause] Four stops, north along Prairie toward the lake. The Keiths are the steadiest family on the street: three brothers, three houses, one great wholesale firm. [short pause] [quietly] But one Monday morning eight years ago, at about this hour, the gentlest of them got up after a sleepless night, put on his hat and coat, and walked out of his front door. [long pause] He walked.

[short pause] Start at his door, where his widow still lives.
scripts.stop:door: [quietly] 1906 Prairie, at daybreak. The widow here is Mrs. Edson Keith. [short pause] Eight years ago her husband, Edson, a merchant, "disappeared from his home at 1906 Prairie avenue about 6 o'clock in the morning". He was 63 and had come to Chicago in 1854. [short pause] [sighs] For at least ten years he had barely slept. [short pause] That last night he paced the halls again, and "his butler found him in a state of deliriousness at 2 AM". [long pause] By six he was gone. Hilda Johnson, the ladies' maid, is first up; Paul Rasmussen, the coachman, is crossing the yard. [short pause] [tenderly] Mrs. Keith comes to the door to look at the weather. Walk north to the brother's house next door.
scripts.stop:brother: [measured] 1900 Prairie, the house of his brother Elbridge, built in 1870 in the Second Empire style that once ruled this street. [short pause] [softly] Elbridge and his wife saw it coming. A few weeks before that Monday they spoke with Edson's wife, [short pause] and she told them, "I … suspect that he was losing control of his mind through long suffering." [short pause] [warmly] His personal secretary said he had never heard him say anything nasty or unkind about anyone. [short pause] That was Edson Keith: the gentle brother, the one who never raised his voice. Elbridge is up early this morning too, and he still passes his brother's door. [short pause] [quietly] Walk north up Prairie, the way Edson went.
scripts.stop:firm: [measured] 1808 Prairie, the Osborn R. Keith house. He and Albert Faxon founded the family firm on Lake Street in 1858, and by the 1880s Edson Keith & Company was selling $4.5 million a year, with two hundred people in Chicago and five hundred more in a Milwaukee factory. [short pause] Three Keith houses on one street, and a fortune. In 1904 the house is Stanley Field's, but the street still calls it a Keith house. [short pause] [softly] Edson walked past it in the dark that Monday, going north, toward the lake. [short pause] [sighs] It is a long walk for a sick man. The house will be razed in 1968, all but the north wall that screens the Glessner courtyard. [short pause] Keep going north to Sixteenth Street.
scripts.stop:lake: [quietly] Sixteenth Street, at the north end of the avenue. East of here, past the railroad, is the lake. [short pause] This is as far as the street goes. [long pause] Edson Keith went on. [short pause] On the beach that Monday morning someone found a hat and a coat. Fishermen on the beach told what they had seen. The papers do not agree where: one says the foot of Sixteenth Street, another the foot of Thirteenth. [short pause] [sadly] All day Monday they searched. The servants worked it out only on Tuesday, when they read it in the newspaper. [long pause] [softly] Stand here and look east at first light. The lake is grey and flat and very large, and it has never given back anything it did not want to.
scripts.ending:dragged: [softly] End of the walk. The news came to the family "with paralyzing suddenness", and the dispatch reported that "the lake is now being dragged for the recovery of the remains." [short pause] Edson Keith had made his will the year before, leaving $300,000 each to his wife Susan and their two sons. [short pause] His wife stayed on at 1906 Prairie, and his brother next door. [long pause] [tenderly] The street remembers him as the gentle brother, the one who never said an unkind word about anyone, who walked out of his own front door at six one Monday morning and went to the lake.
